newsitem.title: USA: Jack Kemp, exuberant vice presidential hopeful.
newsitem.headline: Jack Kemp, exuberant vice presidential hopeful.

text.p: Jack Kemp left professional football more than a quarter of a century ago but, watching the Republican vice presidential challenger spring into action, one might believe he never left the competitive arena.

This one-time quarterback for the San Diego Chargers and Buffalo Bills is 61 but he looks years younger. He is thicker around the middle but still muscular. His once-crew cut hair is long and silver but still thick. He wears eye glasses now.

On the campaign trail -- whether venturing into Harlem or other inner city neighbourhoods where Republicans rarely go or promoting Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole's tax cut plan with missionary zeal -- there is a jaunty bounce to his step and gusto in his speech.
He jogs up stairs. He sheds his jacket, waves to familiar faces. He plunges into crowds to shake hands with a relish.

And there is the ever-present football he still tosses to crowds as he plays the role of the always optimistic top cheerleader for Dole, whom he calls the "quarterback" ever since Dole picked him as his running mate in August.

Kemp was a surprise choice since he and Dole were not close and clashed on policy matters. But they have gotten along fine and Kemp now calls himself Dole's "blocking back," refusing to give up despite trailing the Democratic ticket of President Bill Clinton and Vice President Al Gore in polls.

This is the optimistic persona and sunny outlook he likely will bring to his only debate -- in St. Petersburg, Florida, on Wednesday against Gore, who has an image of stiffness in sharp contrast with the ever-moving, ever-talking Kemp.
It is widely seen as a clash between two men who might face off again as presidential candidates four years hence.

For Kemp, who has shunned the role of "hatchet man" some vice presidential candidates take, the faceoff is one opportunity he hopes will lift the Dole-Kemp team to the kind of come-from-behind victory only sports seem to produce.

Some of the Kemp enthusiasm even has rubbed off on the self-effacing Dole, who told a crowd on Monday after his debate with Clinton that Kemp told him never to look up at the scoreboard since the game is not over until it's over.

"It is the middle of the third quarter and we are a touchdown behind," Kemp said on Sunday. "Clinton is sitting on the ball," he added, suggesting the president was not moving forward while the Dole-Kemp team was.

The Kemp-Gore duel should be a battle of two policy enthusiasts and class debaters. Gore's duel against now Reform Party candidate Ross Perot on the North American Free Trade Agreement on CNN was hailed as a clear victory for Gore.

Kemp, U.S. housing secretary under President George Bush, is a free-enterprise apostle of tax cuts to stimulate the economy who gained attention in Congress as a key figure in passing President Ronald Reagan's 25 percent tax cut in 1981.

Kemp, who played 13 years of football through 1969, parlayed his popularity in Buffalo into 18 years in the House of Representatives. Since leaving as housing secretary in 1993, he has made a small fortune on the speaking circuit.

Kemp was born on July 13, 1935 in Los Angeles. He and his wife Joanne live in the Washington suburb of Bethesda, Maryland. They have four grown children -- Jeffrey, Jennifer, Judith and James -- and 11 grandchildren.
